0.title: Joel: I Will Pour Out My Spirit
0.overview:
The message. Joel takes a national disaster and makes it a summons. A plague of locusts has stripped the land bare, and the prophet says: this is a warning of the day of the LORD, the day God comes to judge, and that day will be far worse; “who can endure it?” (2:11). Then comes the surprise. It is not too late: “return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments” (2:12–13), for the God you have offended “is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (2:13). Those who turn to him find more than a restored harvest: they find God himself in their midst, his Spirit poured out on all his people, and a promise that answers the dreadful question: “everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved” (2:32).

Background: the writer. We know almost nothing about Joel except his name, which means “the LORD is God”, and that he was “the son of Pethuel” (1:1). He knew the temple and its offerings well, and he speaks to Judah and Jerusalem. Everything else is hidden behind his message.

When? Joel names no king, so his date is one of the hardest in the Old Testament to fix, and Christians differ. Some place him early, in the ninth century BC, perhaps when the boy-king Joash was guided by the priests (about 835 BC). On this view the nations he names, Tyre, Philistia, Egypt and Edom, are Judah’s old neighbours, there is no mention of Assyria or Babylon, and his book stands early among the twelve prophets in the Hebrew Bible, beside Amos, who opens with Joel’s words “The LORD roars from Zion” (Amos 1:2; Joel 3:16). Others place him after the exile, perhaps about 500 to 400 BC: the people are led by elders and priests rather than a king, a temple is standing, Judah’s people have been scattered among the nations (3:2), and Greeks appear as slave traders (3:6). This commentary does not press a date. Its notes read “the northerner” (2:20) as foreshadowing Assyria and Babylon, which sits most easily with a date before the exile; but nothing in the message hangs on the year.

The world of the book. Judah lived by its harvests of grain, wine and oil, and by the early rain in autumn and the latter rain in spring. A locust swarm could hold millions of insects, darken the sky and strip a valley in hours. Worse, without grain and wine the daily offerings in the temple stopped (1:9, 13). God had warned in the covenant that disobedience would bring exactly this: “you shall carry much seed into the field and shall gather in little, for the locust shall consume it” (Deuteronomy 28:38). So Joel reads the plague as covenant discipline, and calls for a fast in sackcloth, the ancient sign of mourning and repentance.

The kind of writing. Joel is prophecy in Hebrew poetry, vivid and urgent. Its pictures grow: a real plague becomes an army with the LORD at its head, then the darkening of sun and moon, then the last judgment of the nations. Each day of the LORD in history is a preview of the last one. (In Hebrew Bibles 2:28–32 is chapter 3, and chapter 3 is chapter 4.)

How the book makes its case. The book turns on one verse: before it, warning and lament; after it, promise. First the disaster: wave after wave of locusts, offerings cut off, and “gladness dries up from the children of man” (1:12), so the priests must call a solemn assembly and cry out to the LORD (1:1–20). Then the alarm: the day of the LORD comes like an unstoppable army (2:1–11), and the LORD calls his people to return, gathering everyone from elders to nursing infants while the priests weep, “Spare your people, O LORD” (2:12–17). Then the hinge: “Then the LORD became jealous for his land and had pity on his people” (2:18). He sends rain and harvest and promises, “I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (2:25), and gives the greater gift of his presence: “You shall know that I am in the midst of Israel” (2:27). Afterward he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, and all who call on his name will be saved (2:28–32). Last, he summons the nations who scattered and sold his people to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, a name meaning “the LORD judges”, where their evil is ripe for harvest and winepress (3:1–16). The book ends where the locusts began, but reversed: mountains dripping with sweet wine, a fountain flowing from the house of the LORD, and the last word, “the LORD dwells in Zion” (3:17–21).

Where Christians differ. Is the army of chapter 2 the locusts again, a human army still to come, or the final judgment? This commentary reads it as the real plague described as an invading army, which becomes a picture of greater days of the LORD, from Assyria and Babylon to the last day. And how are the promises of the Spirit and of Zion fulfilled? Many premillennial and dispensational Christians see Pentecost as a first fulfilment, and expect a fuller outpouring and a literal restoration of Israel and Jerusalem at the end of history. This commentary’s view, with many in the Reformed tradition, is that Pentecost began the last days, which run until Christ returns, and that the promises to Zion are fulfilled in Christ and his people and completed in the new creation, because Peter said of Pentecost, “this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16). Both agree that the Spirit has been poured out and that the great day is still ahead.

Where it leads: to Christ. Joel leads to Christ chiefly by promise, and the New Testament says so plainly. At Pentecost, Peter explained what had happened: “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing” (Acts 2:33). The Spirit Joel promised is Christ’s gift to all his people. Paul quotes Joel 2:32, “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13), of calling on Jesus as Lord: the name of the LORD is the name of Jesus. Joel also asked a question no one could answer, “who can endure it?” The cross answers it. When Jesus hung there, “there was darkness over the whole land” (Luke 23:44): the darkness of the day of the LORD fell on him, so that those who call on him find in God “a refuge to his people” (3:16). The harvest and winepress return in Revelation’s judgment by Christ (Revelation 14:15–20; 19:15), and Joel’s fountain becomes “the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1).

For us. Joel teaches us not to waste a disaster: we may not read a particular sin off a particular calamity, but Jesus said every calamity calls us all to repent (Luke 13:1–5). Joel shows what repentance is: not torn clothes but a torn heart, sought together with God’s people, and grounded not in our sorrow but in God’s mercy. He gives hope for lost years, which in Christ are never finally wasted. And he reminds every Christian that the Spirit of the risen Christ lives in us, whoever we are, while we wait for the day when God dwells with his people for ever. Until then, the door is open: call on his name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Has Such a Thing Happened?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God strips away his gifts, he is speaking, and his people must stop, grieve and listen. Joel calls the elders and everyone in the land to hear of a disaster without precedent and to tell it down the generations (vv. 1–3). Wave after wave of locusts has eaten everything, the plague God had warned of in his covenant, and even the drunkards must wake up (vv. 4–7). So the whole land must mourn like a bride widowed on her wedding day: the grain and wine for the temple offerings are gone, the farmers are ashamed, every tree has withered, and gladness itself has dried up from the children of man (vv. 8–12).
verseByVerse.theology: God speaks through disaster, and a people must stop and listen before life can go on as before.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Joel, the son of Pethuel: Hear this, you elders; give ear, all inhabitants of the land! Has such a thing happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children to another generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This disaster is God speaking, and what he says through it must be heard by everyone and handed down to every generation.

The word of the LORD that came to Joel. No date, no king (see the introduction), but the one thing that matters is plain: this is “the word of the LORD”. What follows is not a farmer’s report on crop damage. It is God speaking through a disaster.

Hear this, you elders. Joel calls everyone to attention, from the elders, the leaders and oldest members of the community, to “all inhabitants of the land”. Even the oldest could not remember anything like it. When something unprecedented happens, God’s people should ask what God is saying.

Tell your children of it. The disaster is to be retold for four generations, because God’s dealings are meant to shape the future: not only happy stories of his blessings but sober stories of his judgments, so that children learn to fear the LORD.

How to do it. Start with your own story rather than a lecture: the job lost or the illness, what you learned of God there, and where you were wrong. Tell it while it is fresh, and again years later. Use the ordinary moments Moses named, “when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7): the car journey, the meal, bedtime. When a child asks why something bad happened, say what you know of God and admit what you do not. And keep pointing past your family’s story to the greatest one, the day judgment fell on Christ so that it need not fall on us. The psalmist’s resolve is ours: “We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD” (Psalm 78:4).
verseByVerse.note: Joel's father Pethuel is named nowhere else in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust has eaten. What the swarming locust left, the hopping locust has eaten, and what the hopping locust left, the destroying locust has eaten. Awake, you drunkards, and weep, and wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it is cut off from your mouth. For a nation has come up against my land, powerful and beyond number; its teeth are lions' teeth, and it has the fangs of a lioness. It has laid waste my vine and splintered my fig tree; it has stripped off their bark and thrown it down; their branches are made white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wave after wave of locusts has stripped the land bare, the very curse God had written into his covenant, and its first message is to those who live for their pleasures: wake up.

What the cutting locust left. Four names, and whatever one wave left, the next one ate. To a farming people a swarm of locusts meant famine (see the introduction).

A covenant warning. God had warned Israel of exactly this. Among the curses for breaking the covenant, Moses said, “You shall carry much seed into the field and shall gather in little, for the locust shall consume it” (Deuteronomy 28:38). The locusts were not random bad luck.

Awake, you drunkards. The drunkards would notice first. Some people only wake up to God when their pleasures are taken away.

A nation has come up against my land. The swarm is pictured as an invading army, “powerful and beyond number”, its tiny teeth, multiplied by millions, as destructive as a lion’s. And it is “my land”: God’s own gift to his people.

It has laid waste my vine. The vine and the fig tree were Israel’s pictures of peace and plenty, every man under his own vine and fig tree (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). Stripped of bark, the branches lay bare and white like bones, and would take years to recover.

The true vine. Israel itself was the vine God planted (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7), stripped again and again for bearing no fruit. Jesus took the title for himself: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). He bore the judgment himself, and those joined to him bear fruit that lasts (John 15:16).

Is every disaster a judgment on a particular sin? Joel knew by revelation that this plague was a covenant warning (Deuteronomy 28:38–42). We cannot read a particular sin off a particular disaster; Jesus forbade it (Luke 13:1–5). But every disaster calls all of us to repent.

Uncertain wording. We cannot be sure what the four locust names mean. One is the ordinary word for locust; the rarer ones describe what the insects do. They may be stages of the locust’s growth, different kinds, successive waves, or simply poetry for one plague. On any reading the destruction was total.
verseByVerse.note: The same four names return in 2:25, where God promises to restore the years they ate.

verseByVerse.quote: Lament like a virgin wearing sackcloth for the bridegroom of her youth. The grain offering and the drink offering are cut off from the house of the LORD. The priests mourn, the ministers of the LORD. The fields are destroyed, the ground mourns, because the grain is destroyed, the wine dries up, the oil languishes. Be ashamed, O tillers of the soil; wail, O vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine dries up; the fig tree languishes. Pomegranate, palm, and apple, all the trees of the field are dried up, and gladness dries up from the children of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole land must grieve like a bride widowed on her wedding day, because the harvest has failed, the temple offerings have stopped, and joy itself has dried up.

Lament like a virgin wearing sackcloth. The nation is to grieve like a young bride whose husband has died just as their life together began, wearing sackcloth, the rough cloth of mourning. That is how deeply God’s people should feel this loss.

The grain offering and the drink offering are cut off. The worst result was spiritual. Without grain and wine the daily offerings in the temple stopped, and the fellowship between God and his people expressed in them was cut off.

The fields are destroyed. Grain, wine, oil, wheat, barley, vine, fig, pomegranate, palm and apple: the nation’s whole farming life has collapsed. The ESV notes that in Hebrew “dry up” and “be ashamed” sound alike: as the land dries up, the people are put to shame.

Gladness dries up from the children of man. The last phrase goes deepest. Our joy often rests more than we realise on things God can remove in a day: health, income, food, comfort. The only joy that cannot dry up is joy in God himself. Habakkuk learned to say that “though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines … yet I will rejoice in the LORD” (Habakkuk 3:17–18).

A wedding with no wine. Joel’s scene is a bride without her bridegroom and a land without wine. Jesus’ first sign answered both: at a wedding in Cana, when the wine ran out, he made the best wine of the feast (John 2:1–11), and John the Baptist rejoiced at his coming as the friend of “the bridegroom” (John 3:29). The joy that dries up when God’s gifts are taken returns, and more, when the Bridegroom himself comes.

Uncertain wording. “Virgin” may be translated “young woman” (ESV note), and the word for “bridegroom” more often means husband. Joel may picture a betrothed girl whose intended husband died before the wedding, since a betrothed woman was already counted a wife. Either way it is grief at a life cut off as it began.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Cry Out to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When disaster comes, the right response is to turn to God together and cry out to him, because it warns of a greater day. The priests must lead the way in sackcloth, calling a fast and gathering the whole land to the LORD’s house (vv. 13–14), for the day of the LORD is near: food and joy have vanished from God’s house before their eyes (vv. 15–16). Seed, storehouses and cattle all fail (vv. 17–18). Then Joel himself prays, and the chapter ends with the thirsty animals of the field panting toward God (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: Present disasters are warnings of the great day of the LORD, and the right response is humble, united prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on sackcloth and lament, O priests; wail, O ministers of the altar. Go in, pass the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God! Because grain offering and drink offering are withheld from the house of your God. Consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly. Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land to the house of the LORD your God, and cry out to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests must lead the whole nation in humble, united prayer, because God has promised to hear his people when they cry to him in disaster.

Put on sackcloth and lament, O priests. The priests are to put on sackcloth and spend the night in it. Spiritual leaders cannot call others to humble themselves while remaining comfortable.

Cry out to the LORD. The call to fast and gather rests on a promise: God had said he would hear exactly this. When Solomon dedicated the temple, he prayed that if there was “locust or caterpillar” and God’s people prayed toward that house, God would “hear in heaven your dwelling place and forgive” (1 Kings 8:37, 39). And God answered: “if my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14).

Gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land. The whole community responds together. Churches still need times to fast, pray and seek God together, especially in crisis, not to earn a hearing but because he has promised one, and his Spirit helps us when we do not know how to pray (Romans 8:26).

The priest who wept for us. These priests, lamenting through the night between a guilty people and their God, point to a greater Priest. “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and now “he always lives to make intercession” for those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). Our cries are heard because his were.

verseByVerse.quote: Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is near, and as destruction from the Almighty it comes. Is not the food cut off before our eyes, joy and gladness from the house of our God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The locusts are a foretaste of the day of the LORD, when God comes to judge, and that day is near.

The day of the LORD is near. Here is Joel’s great theme, which runs through the prophets: a day when God steps into history in power, to judge sin and to save his people. Many Israelites assumed it meant judgment on their enemies. The prophets warned that God’s own people would face it too. Amos said, “Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! … It is darkness, and not light” (Amos 5:18).

As destruction from the Almighty it comes. The plague was a preview, a small taste of a far greater judgment. In Hebrew “destruction” sounds like “the Almighty”: destruction is coming from the Almighty. Isaiah used the very same words: “Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come!” (Isaiah 13:6).

Is not the food cut off before our eyes? No food, and no joy in the temple: the festivals had fallen silent.

Facing that day. The New Testament says the day of the Lord is still coming, “like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2), and it shows how anyone can face it. When Jesus hung on the cross, “from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land” (Matthew 27:45). Many Christians have seen in that darkness a sign that the judgment of the day of the LORD was falling on one man in our place. Whatever the sign meant, the gospel is plain: he bore God’s judgment so that those who trust him can face the last day without fear, for “God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: “Destruction” (shod) sounds like the Hebrew for “Almighty” (Shaddai) (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The seed shrivels under the clods; the storehouses are desolate; the granaries are torn down because the grain has dried up. How the beasts groan! The herds of cattle are perplexed because there is no pasture for them; even the flocks of sheep suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drought follows the locusts, and the animals suffer with the people, because human sin brings ruin on the whole creation.

The seed shrivels under the clods. Even next year’s crop shrivelled in the dry ground, and the storehouses stood empty and falling apart.

How the beasts groan! The animals suffer too. The cattle wander about “perplexed”, searching for grass that is not there. Human sin affects all creation, and Paul says that “the whole creation has been groaning together” (Romans 8:22).

A creation waiting. Paul also says why it groans: it waits to be “set free from its bondage to corruption” when God’s children are revealed (Romans 8:21). The first fruits of that freedom have already come up from the ground, in the risen body of Christ (1 Corinthians 15:20). The cattle of Joel 1 are not forgotten in God’s plan for his world.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the first line of verse 17 is uncertain: three of its Hebrew words occur nowhere else in the Old Testament, so “seed”, “shrivels” and “clods” are careful guesses (older versions read that the seed is rotten under the clods). In verse 18 “suffer” may be “are made desolate” (ESV note). The picture is clear: even next year’s harvest is ruined.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O LORD, I call. For fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and flame has burned all the trees of the field. Even the beasts of the field pant for you because the water brooks are dried up, and fire has devoured the pastures of the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joel turns the disaster into prayer, bringing it honestly to the LORD, as even the thirsty animals seem to cry out to God.

To you, O LORD, I call. Having called the people to pray, Joel prays himself, describing exactly what he sees: drought like a fire burning up pastures and trees. This is biblical lament: not a complaint thrown at God from a distance, nor a cheerful pretence that everything is fine, but bringing our pain honestly to God, because we believe he is the only one who can help.

Even the beasts of the field pant for you. Searching dried-up streams, the animals seem to cry out to God. If even the animals look to him, how much more should his people? “As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God” (Psalm 42:1).

Where to turn. Chapter 1 gives no answer yet, but it shows where to turn: not first to fixing things, but to the LORD, together and humbled, remembering that every disaster points to a greater day, which can be faced safely only in Christ. On the cross he said, “I thirst” (John 19:28), so that his people might be led to “springs of living water” (Revelation 7:17).

1.title: Alas for the Day
1.overview:
Where we are. Joel opens without a date or a king and plunges straight into a disaster everyone in Judah has seen. This chapter is the lament that begins the book’s first movement: lament here, the call to return in 2:12–17, and God’s answer from 2:18.

The message. God is speaking through the disaster, and his people must listen. The locusts have taken everything, even the offerings in God’s house and the people’s joy, and that loss is a warning that the day of the LORD is near. The only right answer is to go to God together, humbled, and cry out to him.

Why it was said. A real plague of locusts, followed by drought, had ruined Judah’s grain, wine and oil, the very curse the covenant had warned of (see the introduction). People could have treated it as bad luck and waited for better seasons. Joel will not let them.

How the chapter makes its case. Joel summons the whole land to hear and remember (vv. 1–3) and describes wave after wave of locusts (vv. 4–7). He calls drunkards, priests and farmers to lament, because the offerings have stopped and gladness has dried up (vv. 8–12). Then he calls the priests to gather everyone for a fast (vv. 13–14), names the disaster as a foretaste of the day of the LORD (vv. 15–18), and prays himself, as even the animals pant for God (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. To Christ chiefly by the need it exposes. The chapter shows a people whose joy hangs on gifts that can vanish in a week, and a coming day that no one can face. Christ answers both: he is the true vine and the giver of living water, whose joy “no one will take” from his people (John 15:1; 16:22), and he is the one over whom darkness fell at the cross (Matthew 27:45), bearing that day’s judgment so that those who call on him need not. The priests weeping before God also point, by pattern, to the High Priest who prayed “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7) and still intercedes for his people.

For us. Do not waste a disaster: Jesus said every calamity calls all of us to repent (Luke 13:1–5). When loss comes, go to God, with others and honestly, and let him show you what your joy was resting on. The day of the LORD is still coming, and it can be faced safely only in Christ.
1.theology:
God speaks through disasters, which can be covenant warnings calling his people to attention, and his dealings, including his judgments, are to be taught to the next generations (vv. 1-4; Deut 28:38).

Joy that rests on God's gifts can dry up in a day; lasting joy is found in God himself (vv. 10-12; Hab 3:17-18).

The right response to disaster is humble repentance and prayer by the whole community together, led by its spiritual leaders (vv. 13-14; 1 Kgs 8:37-39; 2 Chr 7:14).

Present judgments preview the great day of the LORD, which is still coming and which Christ bore for his people on the cross (v. 15; Isa 13:6; Amos 5:18; 1 Thess 5:2; Matt 27:45).

Sin affects the whole creation, which groans and looks to God, and biblical lament brings that pain honestly to him in prayer (vv. 18-20; Rom 8:22; Ps 42:1).
1.examples:
Joel's pictures are unforgettable: four waves of locusts, each eating what the last one left; drunkards told to wake up because the wine is gone; fig trees stripped white like bones; and a temple where the offerings have stopped.

Against that devastation a whole nation is called to fast and pray together, while thirsty cattle pant toward heaven.

keyVerse.quote: Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is near, and as destruction from the Almighty it comes.
keyVerse.note: This verse tells us what the locusts mean. The ruined harvest is not the end of the story but a foretaste of the day when God comes to judge, and that day is near. Everything else in the book, the call to return, the promise of the Spirit and the refuge in Zion, answers the question this verse raises.

1.reflection:
Joel tells the elders to pass the story of this disaster down four generations (v. 3). What stories of God’s discipline or mercy in your life or family would be worth telling younger believers, and how could you tell them well?

“Gladness dries up from the children of man” (v. 12). What does your joy rest on that could vanish in a week, and what would it look like to rejoice in the LORD himself (Habakkuk 3:17–18)?

Joel calls the whole community, led by its priests, to fast and cry out together (vv. 13–14). When has your church prayed together in a crisis, and what keeps us from doing it more?

Jesus said disasters call all of us to repent (Luke 13:1–5). How should Christians speak about a national or personal disaster without claiming to know exactly why God sent it?

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Blow a trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm on my holy mountain! verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Day of the LORD Is Great
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day of the LORD is coming, and no one can stand before it in his own strength. The trumpet sounds in Zion because the day is near, dark as a storm cloud on the mountains (vv. 1–2). An army like no other turns a land like Eden into desert; it runs like war horses, keeps perfect ranks, breaks through every defence and enters the houses like a thief (vv. 3–9). Then heaven and earth shake, sun, moon and stars go dark, and the reader learns whose army it is: the LORD is at its head. The section ends with the question the rest of the chapter answers: “who can endure it?” (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The day of the LORD is overwhelming, and no one can endure it in his own strength.

verseByVerse.quote: Blow a trumpet in Zion; sound an alarm on my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD is coming; it is near, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness! Like blackness there is spread upon the mountains a great and powerful people; their like has never been before, nor will be again after them through the years of all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The alarm sounds in Zion because the day of the LORD is coming, dark as a storm cloud, carried by an army like none before.

Blow a trumpet in Zion. The trumpet was a ram’s horn, used to warn a city of attack. It is blown on “my holy mountain”, Zion, where the temple stood. The alarm sounds in the very place of worship, because God himself is coming.

A day of darkness and gloom. A locust swarm really can blot out the sun, and the plague in Egypt was described in similar terms: “such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again” (Exodus 10:14). Zephaniah used Joel’s words for the day of the LORD: “a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness” (Zephaniah 1:15).

The last trumpet. The trumpet will sound once more. “The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). For those who belong to Christ that trumpet is not an alarm but a summons home.

Where Christians differ: who is this “great and powerful people”? Some read it as the locusts of chapter 1 described again as an invading army; others as a human army still to come, such as Assyria or Babylon; others as a picture of the final judgment. This commentary’s view: these are not wholly separate, because Joel moves from the disaster in front of him to the greater judgments it points to, and every day of the LORD in history previews the last one. The likeliest reading is that the real plague is here described in the language of an invading army, and becomes a picture of the greater day to come, with Assyria and Babylon as its first armies.

Uncertain wording. The ESV reads “Like blackness”, but the Hebrew word usually means dawn, and older translations such as the KJV read “as the morning spread upon the mountains”: the swarm covers the hills as fast as first light. Either way the army spreads over the land in moments.

verseByVerse.quote: Fire devours before them, and behind them a flame burns. The land is like the garden of Eden before them, but behind them a desolate wilderness, and nothing escapes them. Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and like war horses they run. As with the rumbling of chariots, they leap on the tops of the mountains, like the crackling of a flame of fire devouring the stubble, like a powerful army drawn up for battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The army turns a land like Eden into desert, a reversal of creation, and nothing escapes it.

Like the garden of Eden. Before the army, the land is “like the garden of Eden”; behind it, “a desolate wilderness”. Sin had already driven humanity out of Eden, and judgment strips away what beauty the world still has. Later the prophets promise the opposite: God “makes her wilderness like Eden” (Isaiah 51:3).

Like the appearance of horses. A locust’s head does look like a small horse’s, and a swarm roars like chariots or a crackling fire. Revelation uses the image for its demonic locusts: “In appearance the locusts were like horses prepared for battle” (Revelation 9:7).

Paradise opened. The way back to Eden is not by our own effort. It was opened by the one who hung on a cross and said to a dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

verseByVerse.quote: Before them peoples are in anguish; all faces grow pale. Like warriors they charge; like soldiers they scale the wall. They march each on his way; they do not swerve from their paths. They do not jostle one another; each marches in his path; they burst through the weapons and are not halted. They leap upon the city, they run upon the walls, they climb up into the houses, they enter through the windows like a thief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No defence can stop this army: it breaks through walls and windows like a thief, as the day of the Lord will.

Like a thief. The army is perfectly disciplined. No soldier breaks rank, and human defences are useless against a judgment God sends: city walls, houses, windows. The phrase “like a thief” is picked up in the New Testament: “the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2). The day of the LORD does not wait for people to be ready. It breaks in.

Be ready. Jesus made the same point about his own return: “you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect” (Matthew 24:44). Readiness is not anxious watching of the skies but a life already turned to him.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 8b is hard. The word translated “weapons” may mean a javelin or missile, and some take it as a water channel; the verb rendered “are not halted” may mean they do not break ranks, while the KJV reads “they shall not be wounded”. On any reading nothing stops them.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth quakes before them; the heavens tremble. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining. The LORD utters his voice before his army, for his camp is exceedingly great; he who executes his word is powerful. For the day of the LORD is great and very awesome; who can endure it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole universe shakes because the LORD himself leads this army, and no one can endure his day.

The earth quakes before them. Earth, sky, sun, moon and stars all shake. The prophets use such language for God’s great interventions in history, and the New Testament for the last day: Jesus said that “the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light” (Matthew 24:29).

The LORD utters his voice before his army. Here is the shock: it is “his army”, with the LORD himself at its head shouting the commands. Israel’s enemy, whether locust or soldier, is God’s instrument.

Who can endure it? No one, in his own strength. Revelation asks the same at the final judgment: “for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?” (Revelation 6:17). Malachi asked it of the Lord coming to his temple: “who can endure the day of his coming?” (Malachi 3:2). The answer begins in the next verse, and is completed in Christ, who endured the darkness of that day on the cross so that those who call on him will stand.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is not too late: the God who leads the army calls his people back to himself, and they may come because of who he is. He asks for a whole-hearted return, torn hearts rather than torn clothes, and grounds the call in his own character, gracious, merciful and slow to anger (vv. 12–13). Joel dares to hope that God will relent and leave enough blessing to restore his worship (v. 14). So the trumpet blows again, this time for prayer: everyone is gathered, from the elders to nursing infants, and the priests weep between the porch and the altar, pleading God’s own name, “Spare your people” (vv. 15–17).
verseByVerse.theology: It is never too late to return to God, because his character is grace, and he calls for torn hearts, not religious show.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet even now," declares the LORD, "return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; and rend your hearts and not your garments." Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even now it is not too late: God calls his people back with a real, inward repentance, and they may come because he is gracious and merciful.

Yet even now. After the terrifying picture of judgment come three of the most hopeful words in the prophets. The army is coming, but the commander of that army himself speaks the invitation: “return to me”. “With all your heart”: not halfway. “With fasting, with weeping, and with mourning”: taking sin seriously. God does not want a casual “sorry” but repentance that feels the weight of what we have done.

Rend your hearts and not your garments. In Israel people tore their clothes to show grief, but clothes can be torn while the heart is untouched. “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

For he is gracious and merciful. Why should anyone dare to return? Because of who God is. These are the words God used of himself to Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), and they became Israel’s great confession; Jonah quoted them, complaining that God was too merciful to Nineveh (Jonah 4:2). He “relents over disaster”: he takes no pleasure in judgment and turns from it gladly when people repent.

The heart that was torn for us. Even our repentance is never whole-hearted enough, but Christ offered the whole-hearted obedience we could not, and it is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), while the Spirit he pours out (v. 28) softens hearts to return. When he died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51): God tore the way open. You do not tear your heart to make God gracious. You can tear it because he already is.

How do I rend my heart? Not by working up strong feelings, which come and go, but by letting God show you the thing itself. Ask him to search you: “Search me, O God, and know my heart!” (Psalm 139:23). Be specific: not “I have not been very loving”, but the sharp word at breakfast, the figure you shaded on the expense claim. Look beneath it: what did you want so badly that you sinned to get it, comfort, approval, control? That is where the heart needs tearing. Confess it plainly, to God, and to the person you wronged where that is needed. Take the promise as true: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). He is just to forgive because Christ has already borne that sin.

A culture of torn garments. Our age is full of public repentance: companies issue statements, celebrities post apologies, movements call on people to acknowledge their guilt. Some of it is sincere, but much is torn garments, a ritual performed for an audience to restore a reputation rather than change a heart. And because the audience is the judge, it never ends: confession everywhere and absolution nowhere, with no one able to say, “You are forgiven; go in peace.” Joel points to a different court. Repentance is turned toward God, not the crowd, and it is safe to be completely honest there because he is “gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love”. A crowd can demand that you tear your clothes. Only God can mend a heart, and in Christ, who bore the sin we confess, he has already spoken the word no crowd can speak.

Does God change his mind? “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19). Scripture says he “relents” to describe his real response to repentance in human terms: his warnings are real, and when people turn, he does what he always purposed to do for those who turn (Jeremiah 18:7–10). He is not surprised or swayed like a man; his unchanging character is the very reason he spares the penitent.
verseByVerse.note: The same confession of God's character returns in Nehemiah 9:17 and Psalms 86:15 and 103:8.

verseByVerse.quote: Who knows whether he will not turn and relent, and leave a blessing behind him, a grain offering and a drink offering for the LORD your God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joel hopes, without presuming, that God will relent and leave enough blessing to restore his worship.

Who knows whether he will not turn and relent? Joel does not take God’s mercy for granted; repentance is not a technique for forcing his hand. But Joel hopes, because he knows God’s character. And he hopes for something specific: that God would “leave a blessing”, enough grain and wine to restore “a grain offering and a drink offering”. The first thing he wants back is not his own comfort but the worship of God, the mark of true repentance.

Who knows? We know. Joel had to say “Who knows?” Those who come to God through Christ can say more, because “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The humility remains, but the uncertainty does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Blow the trumpet in Zion; consecrate a fast; call a solemn assembly; gather the people. Consecrate the congregation; assemble the elders; gather the children, even nursing infants. Let the bridegroom leave his room, and the bride her chamber. Between the vestibule and the altar let the priests, the ministers of the LORD, weep and say, "Spare your people, O LORD, and make not your heritage a reproach, a byword among the nations. Why should they say among the peoples, 'Where is their God?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone, from the oldest to nursing infants, must gather while the priests plead with God to spare his people for the sake of his own name.

Gather the children, even nursing infants. The trumpet blows again, but now it calls to prayer, and no one is excused. The elders, the children, even nursing babies are brought. Even a newly married couple, who under the law had special exemptions (Deuteronomy 24:5), must leave the wedding chamber. When God’s people face his judgment, the whole community stands before him together.

Between the vestibule and the altar. The priests stand between the temple porch and the altar in its court, between the people and God, and weep. Their prayer is a model. They ask for mercy, “Spare your people”; they appeal to God’s ownership, “your people” and “your heritage”; and they appeal to his glory: if his people are destroyed, the nations will mock, “Where is their God?” The best prayers plead God’s own name and honour.

Spare your people. One day another priest stood between a guilty people and God and prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). He did not only plead that God would spare them; he gave himself so that God could, and the nations who ask “Where is their God?” are pointed to him.

Uncertain wording. The phrase translated “a byword among the nations” may also mean that the nations would rule over them (ESV note). Either way the prayer fears the same thing: God’s people disgraced, and his name mocked with them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — I Will Restore the Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers prayer with more than was asked, and the best gift is himself. The turning point comes in verse 18: the LORD becomes jealous for his land and pities his people (v. 18). He gives back what they lost, grain, wine and oil, and drives the northern invader into the desert and the seas (vv. 19–20). Land, animals and people are told not to fear but to rejoice, for the rains have come and the harvest will overflow (vv. 21–24). He will restore the years the locusts ate, and they will know that he is in their midst and that his people will never again be put to shame (vv. 25–27).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers repentance with pity, restoration and his own presence among his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD became jealous for his land and had pity on his people. The LORD answered and said to his people, "Behold, I am sending to you grain, wine, and oil, and you will be satisfied; and I will no more make you a reproach among the nations. "I will remove the northerner far from you, and drive him into a parched and desolate land, his vanguard into the eastern sea, and his rear guard into the western sea; the stench and foul smell of him will rise, for he has done great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the book turns: God becomes jealous for his land, answers his people’s prayer point by point, and drives the invader away.

Then the LORD became jealous for his land. Everything before verse 18 is warning and lament; everything after it is promise. God heard. He became jealous for his land, not in a petty sense but passionately protective, like a husband who will not let his bride be taken, and he “had pity on his people”.

I will no more make you a reproach. God answers their exact request. They prayed not to be a “reproach”, and he says, “I will no more make you a reproach”. They longed for grain and wine for the offerings, and he promises “grain, wine, and oil”, enough to be “satisfied”. God is not reluctant; when his people return, he answers with overflowing generosity.

I will remove the northerner far from you. The “eastern sea” is the Dead Sea and the “western sea” the Mediterranean. Locust swarms have been known to die in the sea and rot on the shore with a terrible smell. The one who “has done great things” in arrogance will be undone.

A jealous love. God’s jealousy for his people reaches its fullest expression in Christ, who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). He will not share his bride with any enemy, and he paid for her with his life.

Uncertain wording. Who is “the northerner”? Locusts rarely came into Israel from the north, so many take it as a sign that Joel’s picture reaches beyond the locusts to the human armies that would come from the north, Assyria and Babylon (see the note on vv. 1–2), while others think an unusual wind drove the swarm. We cannot be sure; either way God removes the threat completely. The ESV notes that “vanguard” is literally “face” and “rear guard” “his end”.

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, O land; be glad and rejoice, for the LORD has done great things! Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield. "Be glad, O children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God, for he has given the early rain for your vindication; he has poured down for you abundant rain, the early and the latter rain, as before. "The threshing floors shall be full of grain; the vats shall overflow with wine and oil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every loss of chapter 1 is answered: land, animals and people are told not to fear but to rejoice, because God has sent the rains and the harvest.

For the LORD has done great things! A beautiful reversal: the enemy “has done great things” (v. 20), but “the LORD has done great things!” The land that mourned in chapter 1 is told to rejoice.

Fear not, you beasts of the field. The animals that groaned and panted for God (1:18, 20) are told not to fear. The burned pastures turn green; the stripped fig tree and vine bear fruit again. Every picture of devastation in chapter 1 is answered with one of restoration, down to the threshing floors full of grain.

The early and the latter rain. Israel depended on two rainy seasons: the early rain in autumn to soften the ground for planting, and the latter rain in spring to bring the crops to maturity. God sends both, and shows the mocking nations (v. 17) that he has not abandoned his people. They are to “rejoice in the LORD your God”, not just in the rain: the gift points to the Giver. And “poured down” prepares us for the greater pouring of verse 28.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “early rain” in verse 23 can also mean “teacher”, and the phrase translated “for your vindication” is literally “for righteousness”. Some older Christian readers took the line as a promise of a teacher of righteousness, and some applied it to Christ; most now read it as rain given in faithfulness to God’s covenant, which fits the rest of the verse.
verseByVerse.note: The early rain fell around October and November, the latter rain around March and April.

verseByVerse.quote: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you. "You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame. You shall know that I am in the midst of Israel, and that I am the LORD your God and there is none else. And my people shall never again be put to shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to make up for the years the locusts ate, and to give the greatest gift of all, himself in the midst of his people.

I will restore to you the years. One of the most comforting promises in the prophets. (The ESV notes that “restore” may be translated “pay back”.) The locusts had eaten more than one harvest: stripped trees and lost seed meant years of loss. God promises to make it up.

My great army, which I sent among you. God does not pretend the disaster came from somewhere else. He sent it as discipline, and the same God restores what it destroyed.

I am in the midst of Israel. Restoration leads to worship: they eat, are satisfied, and “praise the name of the LORD”. And here is the greatest gift: not grain and wine, but God himself. “You shall know that I am in the midst of Israel.” His presence is the heart of every blessing. The promise “my people shall never again be put to shame” comes twice, for emphasis.

God with us. The promise of God in the midst of his people came true in a way Joel could not have pictured: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). In Jesus, God came to live among his people in person, and by his Spirit he now dwells in them.

Lost years in our own lives. Many Christians have found comfort here for lost years: years wasted in sin, lost to sickness, damaged by others or spent under God’s discipline. We should not turn the verse into a promise that every earthly loss will be given back in this life. But the principle is true: the God who disciplines also restores, and in Christ nothing given to him is finally wasted. “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The promise rises beyond the harvest to the gift of God’s own Spirit and to salvation on the last day. Afterward God will pour out his Spirit on all flesh: sons and daughters, old and young, even servants (vv. 28–29). Wonders in heaven and on earth will herald the great and awesome day of the LORD (vv. 30–31). And the chapter ends with the answer to its own question, “who can endure it?”: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved, and among the survivors are those whom the LORD himself calls (v. 32). Peter preached this passage at Pentecost and Paul applied its last verse to Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology: God promises to pour out his Spirit on all his people, and to save everyone who calls on his name, fulfilled from Pentecost onward in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. Even on the male and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beyond the harvest God promises his Spirit on all his people without distinction, a promise Peter says the risen Christ fulfilled at Pentecost.

I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. “Afterward”, beyond the restoration of the land, God promises something new. In the Old Testament the Spirit came on particular people for particular tasks: prophets, judges, kings. Moses once said, “Would that all the LORD’s people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29). Joel says that day is coming.

Even on the male and female servants. Men and women, old and young, even servants: the Spirit will not be the privilege of a few religious professionals but given to all God’s people, down to the lowest in society. Paul rejoiced that Jews and Greeks, slaves and free, “all were made to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:13).

Peter’s sermon. At Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came on the first Christians and they spoke in many languages, Peter said, “this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel”, and quoted this passage, beginning “And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Acts 2:16–17). Where Joel says “afterward”, Peter says “in the last days”, telling his hearers what time Joel meant: the age that began when Christ rose and ascended. And he named who had poured out the Spirit: Jesus, “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing” (Acts 2:33).

The wonder of it. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation and spoke by the prophets now makes his home in fishermen and servant girls, in old men and children, and the ascended Lord who poured him out has never stopped giving him to his people. Every Christian has received this gift: “Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). And “all flesh” reached further than Peter expected, when “the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles” (Acts 10:45).

Does “all flesh” mean every human being? No. Joel defines it at once: sons and daughters, old and young, even servants. It means all kinds of people within God’s people, without distinction of sex, age or rank, and Acts shows it reaching every nation too (Acts 2:39). It is not a promise that every person without exception receives the Spirit, but that no believer is left out.

Does “your daughters shall prophesy” mean women may preach in the church? Women receive the Spirit and his gifts equally (Acts 21:9). The verse does not settle which offices are given to whom; the New Testament teaches that the office of elder and teaching authority over the church belong to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while women serve with great honour.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish tradition reads this as a promise for the age to come, when prophecy, long given to a few, will be given to the whole people; rabbinic midrash links it with Moses’ wish (Numbers 11:29), and many Jewish interpreters take “all flesh” to mean all Israel. Christians share that hope of the Spirit on every one of God’s people, and read it as begun at Pentecost, the gift of the risen Christ to Jews first and then to Gentiles (Acts 2:16; 10:45).

Where Christians differ: do prophecy, dreams and visions continue today? Continuationist Christians hold that these gifts belong to the whole age of the Spirit, which Peter says began at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–18). Cessationists hold that new revelation, by prophecy, dreams and visions, belonged to the founding of the church on “the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians 2:20) and ended when Scripture was complete (Hebrews 1:1–2). This commentary’s view: the second is the better reading. What continues is the Spirit poured on all believers, young and old, men and women, who all speak God’s completed word, and every claimed new word must be tested by Scripture. Godly, Bible-loving Christians hold the continuationist view, and this commentary honours them as brothers; both sides agree that Scripture is complete and that the Spirit is given to every believer.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth, blood and fire and columns of smoke. The sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Signs in heaven and on earth announce the great day of the LORD, and the age of the Spirit before it is the time to call on the Lord.

I will show wonders in the heavens. The outpouring of the Spirit comes before “the great and awesome day of the LORD”, and signs announce it: “blood and fire and columns of smoke”, a darkened sun and a blood-red moon.

Darkness at noon. Some of these signs were already seen when “there was darkness over the whole land” while Jesus hung on the cross (Luke 23:44): the day of the LORD casting its shadow over the one who bore it. The full fulfilment will come at the final day, when Revelation says “the sun became black as sackcloth, the full moon became like blood” (Revelation 6:12).

The point for us. We live between the outpouring of the Spirit and the final day, and this is the time to call on the Lord.

Are “blood moons” signs of the end today? The darkened sun and blood-red moon are the prophets’ language for God’s mighty acts (2:10; Isaiah 13:10). Peter applies them to the age that began at Pentecost (Acts 2:19–20), and Jesus to his coming (Mark 13:24). Lunar eclipses happen regularly; no one can date the end by them (Mark 13:32).

Where Christians differ: how do these verses fit with Pentecost? Many in the Reformed tradition believe Pentecost began the “last days”, the whole age between Christ’s first and second comings, with the signs seen in part at the cross and fully at the end. Others, especially dispensationalists, believe Pentecost was a partial or preview fulfilment, and that a fuller outpouring on Israel, with the cosmic signs, awaits the end of history. This commentary’s view: the first reading is the more likely, because Peter applies the whole prophecy, signs included, to the age that began at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21). Both agree that the Spirit has been poured out and that the great day is still coming.

verseByVerse.quote: And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape, as the LORD has said, and among the survivors shall be those whom the LORD calls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the answer to “who can endure it?”: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved, and Paul says that name is Jesus.

Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved. Not everyone strong enough, good enough or religious enough, but everyone who calls. To call on the name of the LORD is to cry out to God in trust, depending on him alone for rescue.

Paul applies it to Jesus. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10 and applies it directly to Jesus: “if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved”, and then, “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:9, 13). The LORD of Joel is the Lord Jesus. To call on the name of Jesus is to call on the God of Israel, one of the clearest testimonies in the New Testament that Jesus is God.

No distinction. The word “everyone” matters. Paul adds, “For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Romans 10:12). The door is open to anyone, of any nation, background or past, who calls on the Lord.

What this looks like. To call on the name of the LORD is simply to ask him to save you, by name, as someone who cannot save himself. It needs no special words. The tax collector said only, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13), and went home justified. If you have never done it, you can do it today: tell God you have no claim on him, that you trust Jesus, who died for sinners and rose again, to be your Lord and Saviour, and ask him to take you as his own. If you did it long ago, keep calling: when guilt returns at two in the morning, when the diagnosis comes, when temptation is strong, because “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37) is as true on the thousandth day as on the first. And call with others: the first Christians were simply “all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:2).

Those whom the LORD calls. The verse ends with a matching truth: “among the survivors shall be those whom the LORD calls”. We call on the Lord, and the Lord calls us. Peter joined the two at Pentecost: “the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (Acts 2:39). Salvation is freely offered to all, and those who come find that God first drew them. That is grace from beginning to end.

2.title: I Will Pour Out My Spirit
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with a land stripped bare and a prophet crying to God. Chapter 2 holds the whole book’s turning point: the alarm sounds again, the call to return goes out, and then at verse 18 everything changes from warning to promise.

The message. The day of the LORD is coming, and no one can endure it; yet even now God calls his people to return, because he is gracious and merciful. When they do, he gives back far more than they lost: harvests, his own presence among them, his Spirit on all his people, and salvation for everyone who calls on his name.

Why it was said. Judah had just lived through the locust plague and drought of chapter 1, a covenant warning (see the introduction). Joel now shows that the plague was a herald of something greater, and that the God who sent it is ready to forgive.

How the chapter makes its case. The trumpet sounds in Zion, and an unstoppable army turns Eden into desert, with the LORD himself at its head: “who can endure it?” (vv. 1–11). Yet even now God calls for torn hearts, not torn clothes, and the whole people gathers while the priests plead for mercy (vv. 12–17). Then the LORD pities his people, drives off the invader, sends the rains and restores the years the locusts ate, so that they know he is in their midst (vv. 18–27). Afterward he will pour out his Spirit on all flesh, signs will herald the great day, and everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved (vv. 28–32).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise, as plainly as anywhere in the prophets. Peter said of Pentecost, “this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16), and that the risen Jesus had poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33). Paul quotes verse 32 of calling on Jesus (Romans 10:13): the LORD whose name saves is Jesus. The chapter also shows God’s character revealed in Christ, “gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (v. 13), and the question “who can endure it?” is answered at the cross, where he endured the darkness of that day for all who call on him.

For us. It is not too late to return, whatever the years have cost; God does not want a performance but a torn heart, and he is glad to forgive. Every believer, young or old, man or woman, has the Spirit of the risen Christ. And the door is still open: anyone may call on the name of the Lord and be saved.
2.theology:
The day of the LORD is overwhelming, God himself leads its army, and no one can endure it in his own strength (vv. 1-11; Zeph 1:15; Rev 6:17).

It is never too late to return to God, who calls for torn hearts rather than religious display. His gracious and merciful character is the ground of hope for sinners, and true repentance seeks his glory and renewed worship, not only relief (vv. 12-17; Ps 51:17; Exod 34:6; Jonah 4:2).

God answers repentance with pity, restoration and his own presence, and he can redeem lost years (vv. 18-27; Rom 8:28).

God promised to pour out his Spirit on all his people without distinction of sex, age or status, fulfilled at Pentecost by the exalted Christ (vv. 28-29; Acts 2:16-18, 33; 1 Cor 12:13; Rom 8:9).

Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord, who is Jesus, will be saved, and those who call are those whom God calls (v. 32; Rom 10:9-13; Acts 2:39).
2.examples:
The chapter opens with an alarm blown in the temple courts, an army with Eden in front of it and wilderness behind, and locusts coming through the windows like thieves.

Then come torn hearts instead of torn clothes, a bride and groom called from their wedding chamber to a prayer meeting, lost years restored, and the Spirit poured out on servants and grandmothers alike.

keyVerse.quote: Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge between the terror of verses 1–11 and the promises of verses 18–32. The reason it is not too late is God’s own character, the words he spoke of himself to Moses at Sinai. Everything that follows, from restored harvests to the outpoured Spirit, flows from a God who is glad to forgive those who return.

2.reflection:
“Rend your hearts and not your garments” (v. 13). What are some ways we can “tear our garments” today, showing repentance outwardly while the heart stays untouched, and what helps real repentance happen?

Joel grounds the call to return in God’s character, gracious, merciful and slow to anger (v. 13). How does knowing what God is like make it easier, or harder, for you to confess sin honestly?

“I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten” (v. 25). What lost years have you or people you know grieved over, and what can we rightly hope for from God about them without promising more than he has promised?

Peter says the Spirit promised in verses 28–29 has been poured out on all believers. How should the truth that every Christian, young or old, man or woman, has the Spirit shape the way your church values and uses its members?
