verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — I Will Enter into Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will call the nations to account for every wrong done to his people, because he counts their wrongs as done to him. When he restores Judah and Jerusalem, he will gather all nations to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, whose name means “the LORD judges”. The charges are specific and terrible: they scattered his people, divided up his land, gambled for captives, and traded a boy for a prostitute and a girl for wine (vv. 1–3). Tyre, Sidon and the Philistines are singled out for looting God’s treasures and selling the people of Judah to the Greeks. God will bring the captives back and return the slave traders’ payment on their own heads (vv. 4–8).
verseByVerse.theology: God takes personally every wrong done to his people, and he will judge it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem, I will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. And I will enter into judgment with them there, on behalf of my people and my heritage Israel, because they have scattered them among the nations and have divided up my land, and have cast lots for my people, and have traded a boy for a prostitute, and have sold a girl for wine and have drunk it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God restores his people, he will call every nation to account for what it did to them, because he counts their wrongs against his people as wrongs against himself.

In those days and at that time. The chapter continues the promises of chapter 2: “in those days” is the time when God pours out his Spirit and saves all who call on his name. When God rescues the oppressed, he must deal with the oppressors.

The Valley of Jehoshaphat. God summons “all the nations” to court. The name recalls King Jehoshaphat, in whose days a great alliance of nations came against Judah, and God told the people, “the battle is not yours but God’s”; while Judah sang praises, God routed the enemy (2 Chronicles 20:15, 22). This is the place where God himself deals with the nations.

My people and my heritage Israel. God speaks of “my people”, “my heritage” and “my land”. To attack God’s people is to attack God. Jesus said the same of his followers: “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).

Traded a boy for a prostitute. Conquerors gambled for captives as prizes, traded a boy for a night with a prostitute and sold a girl for a jug of wine. Human beings made in God’s image were treated as cheap goods for their captors’ pleasures. God sees, remembers and will judge. There is great comfort here for every victim of trafficking, abuse and cruelty: the Judge of all the earth has noticed.

What is a child worth? Every age prices people, and ours does it by the market: we measure a life by its productivity and quietly treat those who cannot produce, the very old, the disabled, the unborn, as costs. The Bible will not allow it. A human being bears the image of God (Genesis 9:6), and that has no price. Then the gospel names the price God himself paid for his people: “you were ransomed … not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Whatever the market says you are worth, that is what you cost him.

Uncertain wording. No valley called Jehoshaphat is mentioned anywhere else in the Old Testament, and we do not know where it was. Later tradition linked it with the Kidron Valley beside Jerusalem. Since the name means “the LORD judges”, Joel may be naming the place by what happens there rather than pointing to a spot on a map.
verseByVerse.note: “Jehoshaphat” means “the LORD judges”, so the name itself announces what happens there.

verseByVerse.quote: "What are you to me, O Tyre and Sidon, and all the regions of Philistia? Are you paying me back for something? If you are paying me back, I will return your payment on your own head swiftly and speedily. For you have taken my silver and my gold, and have carried my rich treasures into your temples. You have sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks in order to remove them far from their own border. Behold, I will stir them up from the place to which you have sold them, and I will return your payment on your own head. I will sell your sons and your daughters into the hand of the people of Judah, and they will sell them to the Sabeans, to a nation far away, for the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will repay the cities that looted his treasures and sold his people into slavery, giving them back exactly what they did.

What are you to me, O Tyre and Sidon? Tyre and Sidon were the great trading cities of the coast to the north, and Philistia lay along the coast to the south-west. God asks with irony whether they are trying to get even with him.

You have taken my silver and my gold. They had looted treasures, perhaps even from God’s temple, and carried them into their own “temples” (the ESV notes this may be “palaces”), as trophies for their gods.

You have sold the people of Judah. The worst charge is slave trading. Amos made the same accusation against Gaza and Tyre (Amos 1:6, 9). Tyre and the Philistine cities sold captured Judeans to Greek traders, who shipped them far across the sea so they could never return.

I will return your payment on your own head. The captives will be stirred up to return, and the slave traders will suffer what they inflicted: their own children sold to the Sabeans of southern Arabia, as far to the south as the Greeks were to the west. In the centuries that followed, Tyre and Sidon were conquered and many of their people were themselves sold as slaves. God’s justice is exact: “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (Obadiah 15).

Leave it to God. This is not permission for believers to take revenge: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). It is a promise that God himself will do what is right. Christ showed the way: when he suffered, “he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Multitudes in the Valley of Decision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nations gather for war, but they will meet a Judge, not an opponent. Joel mockingly summons them to arm themselves, beating ploughshares into swords and calling even the weak to fight, while he prays for the LORD’s own warriors to come down (vv. 9–11). God will sit in the Valley of Jehoshaphat to judge (v. 12). Their evil is ripe like a harvest and overflowing like a full winepress, and the multitudes stand in the valley of decision, where God gives his verdict (vv. 13–14). Sun and moon go dark, the LORD roars from Zion and heaven and earth shake, but he is a refuge and stronghold for his people (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The final judgment of the nations is certain, and in that day God himself is his people's refuge.

verseByVerse.quote: Proclaim this among the nations: Consecrate for war; stir up the mighty men. Let all the men of war draw near; let them come up. Beat your plowshares into swords, and your pruning hooks into spears; let the weak say, "I am a warrior." Hasten and come, all you surrounding nations, and gather yourselves there. Bring down your warriors, O LORD. Let the nations stir themselves up and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat; for there I will sit to judge all the surrounding nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are summoned to arm themselves for a battle already lost, because God is not coming to fight them but to sit and judge them.

Consecrate for war. The scene shifts to a great final battle, and God challenges the nations to prepare. (The ESV notes it may be read “Consecrate a war”, as though it were a holy war.) The irony is heavy: the nations think they are fighting God’s people; in fact they are being summoned to God’s courtroom.

Beat your plowshares into swords. Verse 10 turns a famous prophecy upside down. Isaiah and Micah promised that in the last days the nations “shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks” (Isaiah 2:4; Micah 4:3). Joel mockingly tells the nations to do the opposite and let even the weakest pretend to be a warrior. It will make no difference.

Bring down your warriors, O LORD. In the middle of the challenge the prophet prays. God has his own army, the hosts of heaven: the battle is between the nations and God.

There I will sit to judge. The nations come for war, but God does not stand up to fight. He sits on the judge’s seat. The Psalms picture the same scene: when the kings of the earth rise against God, “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4). The outcome was never in doubt.

The King on Zion. The same psalm names God’s answer to the raging nations: “I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill”, the Son to whom he gives the nations as his heritage (Psalm 2:6–8). The New Testament says that King is Jesus (Acts 4:25–28; 13:33). He will judge the nations, and under his reign, not by our efforts, swords will at last become ploughshares.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah and Micah reverse this: swords into ploughshares.

verseByVerse.quote: Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Go in, tread, for the winepress is full. The vats overflow, for their evil is great. Multitudes, multitudes, in the valley of decision! For the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations’ evil is ripe like a harvest and overflowing like a full winepress, and in the valley of decision God gives his verdict.

Put in the sickle. Two pictures from farming describe the judgment: the grain harvest, “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe”, and the grape harvest, “Go in, tread, for the winepress is full.” The overflowing vats picture overflowing evil. The nations’ wickedness has reached its full measure, and the time for judgment has come.

The same pictures in Revelation. An angel calls, “Put in your sickle, and reap, for the hour to reap has come, for the harvest of the earth is fully ripe” (Revelation 14:15), and the grapes are thrown “into the great winepress of the wrath of God” (Revelation 14:19). It is Christ himself who “will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty” (Revelation 19:15). Jesus taught that “The harvest is the end of the age” (Matthew 13:39). God is patient, but he does not wait for ever.

The Judge who drank the cup. The one who will tread the winepress of wrath first drank the cup of it himself. In Gethsemane he prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). Because he drank it, those who belong to him will not.

Multitudes, multitudes, in the valley of decision! The phrase is often used as a call to decide for Christ, a good call. But in Joel the “decision” is God’s: his verdict. That makes the call to decide now all the more urgent. Today is the day to call on the name of the Lord (2:32). On the last day the only decision that matters will be God’s, and it will turn on whether we belong to Christ by faith.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “decision” means something cut or decided, a verdict, but the same word is used elsewhere of a threshing sledge, the heavy board with sharp teeth dragged over grain (Isaiah 41:15). Joel may intend both: the valley where the verdict is given and where the harvest is threshed. Either way the decision belongs to God.

verseByVerse.quote: The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining. The LORD roars from Zion, and utters his voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth quake. But the LORD is a refuge to his people, a stronghold to the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice that shakes heaven and earth is terror to God’s enemies and shelter to his people.

The sun and the moon are darkened. The cosmic darkness of 2:10 and 2:31 comes over the scene. All creation holds its breath before the Judge.

The LORD roars from Zion. God speaks like a roaring lion, and the universe shakes. Amos opens his book with the same words: “The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem” (Amos 1:2). For God’s enemies this roar is terror.

But the LORD is a refuge to his people. Then comes the word “But”. The God whose voice shakes heaven and earth is a safe place for those who belong to him; the voice that terrifies the nations comforts his people, because the one roaring is their Father. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psalm 46:1). “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10).

A refuge with a name. For Christians this refuge has a name. Those who have called on the name of the Lord Jesus have fled to him for refuge, and “God has not destined us for wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–21 — The LORD Dwells in Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends with God at home among his people in a renewed land. They will know that the LORD dwells in Zion, and Jerusalem will be holy, never again trampled by strangers (v. 17). Everything the locusts took is given back in overflowing measure: mountains drip with sweet wine, hills flow with milk, dry streambeds run with water, and a fountain flows from the house of the LORD (v. 18). Egypt and Edom, symbols of Israel’s enemies, become desolate for the innocent blood they shed, while Judah is inhabited for ever (vv. 19–20). God will deal with the blood that has gone unanswered, and the last words are the best: “the LORD dwells in Zion” (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends with God dwelling among his people in a renewed and holy creation, flowing with life.

verseByVerse.quote: "So you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who dwells in Zion, my holy mountain. And Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall never again pass through it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of all God’s judging is that he should live among his people in a city made holy.

Who dwells in Zion, my holy mountain. After the judgment comes the purpose of it all: “you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who dwells in Zion.” God’s great purpose is to live among his people. Jerusalem will be holy, set apart for God and cleansed of evil, and “strangers shall never again pass through it”: no invader or unclean enemy will trample it again.

The holy city. Hebrews tells Christians, “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). The holiness Joel promised is given now to all who are in Christ, and completed in the new creation, where “nothing unclean will ever enter it” (Revelation 21:27).

Where Christians differ: how should Christians understand these promises about Judah and Jerusalem? Many premillennial and dispensational Christians believe they describe a future restoration of the nation of Israel and the city of Jerusalem in a coming earthly kingdom. Many in the Reformed tradition believe they are fulfilled in Christ and his people, the true Zion, and completed in the new creation, where “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3). This commentary’s view: the second is the more likely reading, because it is how the New Testament itself handles the promises to Zion. Both views share the same hope: a day when God dwells with his people in perfect holiness and peace.

verseByVerse.quote: "And in that day the mountains shall drip sweet wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the streambeds of Judah shall flow with water; and a fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD and water the Valley of Shittim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruin of chapter 1 is reversed: wine, milk and water flow, and at the centre a fountain springs from God’s house.

The mountains shall drip sweet wine. In chapter 1 the wine was cut off, the brooks dried up and the cattle panted for water. Here the mountains drip sweet wine, the hills flow with milk and every dry streambed runs with water: a land more fruitful than the land of milk and honey.

A fountain shall come forth from the house of the LORD. At the centre is a fountain flowing from God’s house: the source of all this life is his presence. Ezekiel saw water flowing from the temple and bringing life wherever it went (Ezekiel 47:1), and Zechariah saw “living waters” flowing out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8).

The fountain fulfilled. The Bible ends with this fountain fulfilled. John saw “the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1). And Jesus offers that water now: “whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again” (John 4:14).

Uncertain wording. We do not know for certain where “the Valley of Shittim” was. Shittim means acacia trees, which grow in dry ground, so it is probably a dry valley, perhaps running down toward the Dead Sea. If it is linked with the Shittim where Israel sinned with Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:1), the place of Israel’s old sin becomes a place of life. Either way, the fountain reaches the driest places.

verseByVerse.quote: "Egypt shall become a desolation and Edom a desolate wilderness, for the violence done to the people of Judah, because they have shed innocent blood in their land. But Judah shall be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem to all generations. I will avenge their blood, blood I have not avenged, for the LORD dwells in Zion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Violence against the innocent will be answered, God’s people will dwell secure for ever, and the book ends with its best news: the LORD dwells in Zion.

Egypt shall become a desolation. Egypt and Edom stand for the long line of Israel’s enemies, from the slavery in Egypt to Edom’s betrayal of its brother nation. Their land will become the wilderness Judah once was, because of the innocent blood they shed. God does not overlook violence against the innocent.

Jerusalem to all generations. Empires turn to wilderness, but God’s people endure for ever. Christians share that hope: they are receiving “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).

I will avenge their blood. Much innocent blood has never been avenged. The martyrs in Revelation cry, “how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10). God answers: he will. “For he who avenges blood is mindful of them; he does not forget the cry of the afflicted” (Psalm 9:12). For anyone who has suffered violence, this is not a call to settle the account yourself, but an assurance that it will be settled; meanwhile, if you are in danger now, tell someone you trust and seek help that same day.

For the LORD dwells in Zion. The book began with locusts, famine, drought and weeping; it ends with God living among his people. Everything Joel promised, the restored harvest, the outpoured Spirit, salvation for all who call, judgment on evil and the fountain of life, flows from this one reality: God with us. That is what Jesus came to bring, and what he will bring in fullness when he returns.

Where Christians differ: does “Judah shall be inhabited forever” point to a modern state? Christians who expect a future for national Israel in God’s plan read it of the land and people of Israel, and they are honoured brothers. This commentary’s view: it speaks of the eternal security of God’s people in the new creation, not of a modern state. All agree that God’s people will dwell with him for ever.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 21a is difficult. The ESV notes that it may be read “I will acquit their bloodguilt that I have not acquitted”, which would be a promise of cleansing for God’s own people rather than vengeance on their enemies. Either reading ends in God setting everything right.

3.title: The Valley of Decision
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with the Spirit poured out and the promise that everyone who calls on the LORD will be saved. Chapter 3 (chapter 4 in Hebrew Bibles) carries the same “in those days” forward to its end: the judgment of the nations and the LORD dwelling with his people.

The message. God will set the world right. The nations that scattered, plundered and sold his people will stand before him, and their evil, ripe for harvest, will be judged. But the same voice that shakes heaven and earth is a refuge for his people, and the story that began with a stripped and thirsty land ends with wine on the mountains, a fountain from God’s house, and God himself living among them.

Why it was said. Judah was small and preyed on: its neighbours had looted its treasures and sold its children as slaves far away (see the introduction). God’s people needed to know that he had seen it, and that history would not end with the oppressors on top.

How the chapter makes its case. When God restores his people, he summons all nations to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, “the LORD judges”, for scattering and selling his people (vv. 1–3), and repays Tyre, Sidon and Philistia in kind (vv. 4–8). The nations arm for a battle already lost, for God sits to judge (vv. 9–12); their evil is ripe for harvest in the valley of decision (vv. 13–14), and the LORD who roars from Zion is his people’s refuge (vv. 15–16). Then the land is renewed, a fountain flows from God’s house, violence is avenged, and the book ends, “the LORD dwells in Zion” (vv. 17–21).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by the character of God revealed in him. The judge of the nations is the man God has appointed (Acts 17:31), before whom “will be gathered all the nations” (Matthew 25:32). Revelation takes up Joel’s sickle and winepress for Christ’s judgment (Revelation 14:14–20; 19:15), yet he first drank the cup of wrath himself, and so is the refuge of verse 16 for all who call on him. And Joel’s fountain becomes “the river of the water of life … flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1), where at last “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

For us. Every victim of cruelty can know that God has seen and will judge, so we need not take revenge. Every sinner can know that the Judge is also a refuge, and the time to run to him is now, before the day of decision. And every believer can live in hope: the story ends not with locusts but with God at home among his people.
3.theology:
God takes every wrong done to his people as done to himself, and he will judge cruelty, slavery and the treatment of people as goods; vengeance is his, not ours (vv. 1-8; Matt 25:40; Amos 1:9; Obad 15; Rom 12:19).

No human power can stand against God; the nations' war is folly before the Judge (vv. 9-12; Ps 2:4; 2 Chr 20:15).

The final judgment is certain and will come when evil is ripe, carried out by Christ (vv. 13-14; Rev 14:15-20; 19:15; Matt 13:39).

The God whose voice shakes heaven and earth is the refuge of his people, and in Christ believers are not destined for wrath (v. 16; Ps 46:1; Prov 18:10; 1 Thess 5:9).

God's final goal is to dwell among a holy people in a renewed creation flowing with life, fulfilled in Christ and consummated in the new Jerusalem (vv. 17-18; Heb 12:22; Rev 21:3, 27; 22:1; John 4:14).

God will avenge innocent blood and set all things right (vv. 19-21; Rev 6:10; Ps 9:12).
3.examples:
The chapter sets all the nations in a valley no map can find, where a boy was traded for a prostitute and a girl for a jug of wine, and farm tools are hammered into swords for a battle already lost. The Judge sits down while the armies arrive, and his lion's roar terrifies enemies and shelters his children.

It ends with mountains dripping wine where locusts once stripped the vines, and a fountain flowing from God's house into the valley where Israel once sinned.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD roars from Zion, and utters his voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth quake. But the LORD is a refuge to his people, a stronghold to the people of Israel.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on the word “But”. The same God whose voice judges the nations and shakes the universe is a safe place for those who belong to him. That is the hope the book has been building toward since “who can endure it?” (2:11), and in Christ it is open to everyone who calls on his name.

3.reflection:
God says those who sold his people “traded a boy for a prostitute” and “sold a girl for wine” (v. 3). In what ways does our own culture put a price on people, and how does the cross change the way we value the weak and vulnerable?

Joel promises that God will repay evil exactly (vv. 4–8, 21). How does trusting God to judge free us from taking revenge, and what does that look like when someone has seriously wronged you?

“The LORD roars from Zion … But the LORD is a refuge to his people” (v. 16). Why do we need to know God both as Judge and as refuge, and how does Jesus hold the two together?

Joel ends not with harvests but with “the LORD dwells in Zion” (v. 21). How does the hope of God living with his people for ever (Revelation 21:3) change the way you face loss, injustice and waiting now?
